transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-15
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 62m
Attendees: Max Chen (Redwood AE), Sofia Patel (Redwood SE), Amir Hassan (Redwood Product), Liam O'Connor (NovaEdge SRE), Rosa Martínez (NovaEdge Lead ML Eng), Daniel Park (Platform Eng), Priya Singh (Security)

[00:00] Max Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Is this audio sounding ok?
[00:08] Liam O'Connor: Yeah can hear you, good.
[00:12] Max Chen: Cool. Quick agenda — we'll run through a short ops runbook in Console, show request -> trace -> log playback, then a KV-cache fallback scenario, and leave time for security questions. Sofia will drive demos.
[00:27] Sofia Patel: Hi all, I'll share my screen. Quick note — transcription might mangle some product names, you might see "Rudwood" or something, apologies in advance.
[00:35] Rosa Martínez: That happens. No worries.

[02:02] Sofia Patel: Alright, this is the Console request lookup. We'll search by request id, or you can filter by route, model, or token count. I'm pulling up a synthetic request that shows a degradation pattern.
[02:18] Daniel Park: Can you show how it ties back to the actual logs in our infra? We need linking to our CloudWatch / Splunk events.
[02:26] Sofia Patel: Yes. We have two options — out-of-the-box we attach the request_id to your request metadata and you can push logs via the log-forwarder. For customers with VPC peering we can also configure a private egress collector. Here I'll click "Open request" — you can see the header with start time, latency, and model variant.
[03:00] [Auto-note] Transcript generator: 'Open request' button clicked

[04:10] Sofia Patel: Now the trace timeline — it shows per-step durations: routing, model exec, KV cache lookup, and response formatting. Here we have a big spike on model execution at 0.8s.
[04:30] Liam O'Connor: That spike is what we saw in production around 13:42 UTC, yes. That corresponds to a user-facing latency bump.
[04:40] Sofia Patel: Exactly. If we click into the model node, you can see the full token timing and the kernel selection hint. We also surface the quantization profile used — in this run it's a 4-bit QK algo.

[06:05] Rosa Martínez: Sometimes the console shows weird labels for KV cache — our team saw it say "KV cash" earlier — is that a transcription issue or a UI bug?
[06:16] Sofia Patel: That's a good catch, I've seen the auto-transcription in the playback mislabel things. UI shows the correct "KV cache" label; the S3 transcript export has some OCR noise if you use the automated captions. We'll flag the export.

[08:00] Sofia Patel: Next — request replay. We can replay a request in a sandboxed runner that has the same model variant pinned. Here I'll run a replay with prefix caching enabled, and then show a replay with cache cold.
[08:25] [Playback started]
[09:12] Sofia Patel: Replay one — cache warm — you can see latency ~120ms in the console. Replay two — cache cold — latency jumps to ~820ms and you can see multiple Fetches to the KV store in the trace.
[09:35] Daniel Park: How does that map to our Redis TTL? We set small TTLs for some prefixes.
[09:42] Sofia Patel: We annotate the trace with the cache hit/miss and the metadata includes the key namespace. If your Redis TTL is short you'll see high miss rate. We can also surface a cache miss rate metric per-prefix.

[11:00] Amir Hassan: One useful runbook step we've recommended is an automated fallback: if model exec > 600ms fall back to a cheaper smaller model variant and flag the sample for eval. We can demo that flow.
[11:18] Max Chen: Sofia can you trigger a canary fallback?
[11:22] Sofia Patel: On it. I'm toggling a policy — we set threshold 600ms, fallback variant 'redwood-small-2b', and the routing policy will try small-2b for that request. Watch the trace: you'll see a second call to the alternative endpoint and the console correlates both attempts.
[12:15] [Event] Canary fallback invoked; second model called
[12:34] Rosa Martínez: Nice, and does the console automatically merge the traces into a single logical request?
[12:40] Sofia Patel: Yes — it presents them as an "attempt sequence" with an overall outcome. You can expand each attempt for timing and token diffs.

[14:00] Liam O'Connor: From a debugging perspective, we need deeper correlation to our request ids — we have a distributed trace id we use across services. Can we inject that into the Redwood request metadata?
[14:12] Sofia Patel: Absolutely, you can supply X-Request-ID or X-Trace-ID headers and we'll store them as part of the request. That allows you to search in Console by your trace id.

[16:05] Priya Singh: Security question — on private deployments, where are logs stored? What about keys and KMS?
[16:14] Max Chen: For Redwood Private you can choose the control plane in your VPC or our private package. Keys can be integrated with your KMS/HSM. Audit logs are available and retention is configurable per contract. We can deliver an SOC2 summary and architecture doc.
[16:40] Priya Singh: Do you support customer-managed S3 for audit exports? We prefer not to push PII outside.
[16:48] Sofia Patel: Yes, you can export audit logs to a customer-managed S3 bucket in the same region or set up a direct syslog/forwarder. We also support per-tenant encryption with your KMS CMKs.

[18:30] Rosa Martínez: Can we run an ingest of our real workload, but anonymized? We want to see end-to-end latencies and cost estimations.
[18:40] Max Chen: That's the typical pilot. If you share a scrubbed sample and an expected QPS distribution we can run a 24-48h baseline to give latency/cost numbers and model recommendations via Optimize.

[20:00] Sofia Patel: Now showing the error analysis tab — you can group by error type: model reject, formatting error, timeout, and fallback invoked. Each group has representative requests and an inline diff view so you can see token-level differences.
[20:28] Daniel Park: Do errors include stack traces from the runtime? We sometimes need the kernel-level exception to debug a segfault in custom ops.
[20:38] Sofia Patel: For hosted and dedicated we capture runtime errors and include the runtime code path id. For on-prem/private with full debug enabled we can capture extended traces — but note that requires debug kernel logging which increases disk and possible PII surface, so it must be enabled per agreement.

[23:10] [Noise / crosstalk] Someone: mm-hm, yeah

[24:00] Sofia Patel: Demoing request logs linkage — I click "open logs" and it jumps to your log-forwarder link. You can view raw logs side-by-side with the request timeline which makes root cause triage faster.
[24:20] Rosa Martínez: If we have a high volume of small requests, what's the cost hit of streaming all logs?
[24:28] Sofia Patel: We recommend sampling at 1% for full logs and retaining full traces for errors and anomalies. There are configurable sampling policies in Console. Also Optimize will recommend batching params to reduce per-token compute cost.

[26:00] Liam O'Connor: On the runbook itself, can we set an automated pager rule? For example: if error rate > 2% for 10 minutes AND latency p95 > 500ms then page platform on-call?
[26:12] Sofia Patel: Yes, Console integrates with PagerDuty/Slack and you can define composite alerts. We also provide templated runbook entries you can copy into your ops doc.

[28:00] Max Chen: Let's walk through a hypothetical incident. Sofia triggers a synthetic spike and we'll follow the runbook.
[28:10] [Synthetic spike triggered]
[28:30] Sofia Patel: Spike injected. Console shows degradation, alert fires, request sampling shows cache miss and model exec spike. Step one in runbook: check cache miss rate. Step two: if miss rate high, check Redis keys and TTLs. Step three: if model exec is slow, fallback to small model and create a regression eval.
[29:00] Rosa Martínez: For evaluation, can the console push flagged requests into our human-in-the-loop eval queue?
[29:10] Amir Hassan: Yes, flagged requests can be exported to your eval set. You can configure thresholds to auto-sample for human review.

[31:00] Daniel Park: On metrics retention: what's the default retention for traces and token-level timings?
[31:08] Sofia Patel: Hosted tier retains detailed traces for 30 days by default; you can extend that via add-on. Dedicated typically offers longer retention per contract and Private you control retention.

[33:30] Rosa Martínez: A small nit — some of our developers found the "Attempt sequence" UI a little confusing when there are >3 fallbacks. Is there a way to collapse by outcome?
[33:42] Sofia Patel: We do have a grouped view toggles — I'll enable the "collapse by final outcome" option in the demo. That should make long attempt chains easier to parse.

[36:00] [Silence while screen changed] 

[37:10] Liam O'Connor: Are there limits to the size of logs you can attach per request? We occasionally have multi-10MB payloads.
[37:20] Sofia Patel: We cap inline attachments to 5MB in the Console to keep the UI responsive. For larger artifacts we store a pointer to your object store; Console will fetch it on demand.

[39:00] Priya Singh: For SOC2 evidence, do you provide architecture diagrams and a list of subservice auditors?
[39:07] Max Chen: Yes, we have a package: SOC2 summary, encryption at rest/in-transit docs, KMS integration guide, and a list of third-party audits. I'll attach that after the call.

[41:30] Rosa Martínez: Can we run the KV-cache fallback on a percentage of requests for a gradual rollout?
[41:40] Sofia Patel: Absolutely — rollout controls support percentage-based routing and canary windows. You can also set automatic rollback based on quality regression alerts.

[44:00] Sofia Patel: Quick note on cost observability — Console shows token-level cost per request and aggregates by route/model. We can export per-token cost to your billing export so finance can map to product lines.
[44:18] Daniel Park: Great, we need that to charge internal teams.

[46:00] [Slight lag]

[47:10] Max Chen: Ok, high-level recap before Q&A: 1) Console links requests -> traces -> logs, 2) replay and sandboxed replays for debugging, 3) KV-cache hit/miss visibility and fallback policies, 4) runbook + alerting templates and PD integration, 5) security options and audit exports.
[47:30] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. Who's owning the pilot checklist?
[47:36] Max Chen: I'll own the pilot checklist from our side. Action items: I'll send the checklist + SOC2 pack. Rosa will provide the anonymized logs. Sofia will prepare the KV-cache demo script.

[49:00] Rosa Martínez: One more question — do you have a preferred scrub pattern for logs? We want to minimize manual work.
[49:10] Sofia Patel: We have a python scrubber template that strips PII and replaces tokens. I'll share the repo link.

[51:20] Daniel Park: Any blockers for VPC peering? We have strict egress constraints and need to route via a NAT with proxy.
[51:32] Max Chen: We can work with your infra team. We'll need details on egress IP ranges, proxy, and allowed ports. That will inform whether we recommend Dedicated or Private.

[54:00] [Quick technical aside] Sofia Patel: If you want ultra-low jitter, Dedicated with pinned GPU pools is recommended. For regulated workloads Private is best. Hosted is easiest to start.

[56:30] Priya Singh: For legal, we'll need a data processing addendum and details on subprocessors.
[56:40] Max Chen: Noted — I'll attach our DPA and subprocessors list with the SOC2 docs.

[58:10] Rosa Martínez: Ok, recap on deadlines: I'll get logs by Friday the 18th; Max you'll send SOC2 and runbook template by tomorrow the 16th; Sofia will prep the demo script by 17th.
[58:25] Max Chen: Correct. We aim to kick off pilot week of 2026-09-22.

[60:00] [Closing chatter] 
[61:00] Max Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via Slack and attach the artifacts.
[61:08] Sofia Patel: Thanks, bye.
[61:12] Rosa Martínez: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
